laws: N.J.S.A. 2C:40-28 (P.L.2017, c.315): operating a drone in a way that endangers another's life or property is a disorderly persons offense; flying on or near a correctional facility without authorization in a way that endangers its safety/security is a 4th-degree crime (3rd-degree if used to surveil it); knowingly interfering with first responders is a 4th-degree crime.
parks: NJ State Park Service Policy 2.38 prohibits drone operation on all lands and waters administered by the State Park Service unless specifically approved under N.J.A.C. 7:2-1.4(b). NJDOT notes recreational requests are not considered; commercial use may be possible via a Policy Waiver Request and Special Use Permit (e.g., Liberty State Park requires Part 107, registration, flight plan).
https://njdotlocalhub.nj.gov/aeronautics/unmanned-aircraft-systems/
NJDEP Special Use Permit guidelines (UAV checklist)
https://dep.nj.gov/wp-content/uploads/parksandforests/SUP-Guidelines-w.fillable-ops-plan-2023.pdf

laws: 18 Pa.C.S. § 3505 (Act 78 of 2018): unlawful to intentionally/knowingly use a drone to surveil a person in a private place or to place a person in reasonable fear of bodily injury (summary offense, fine up to $300), or to deliver contraband (2nd-degree felony).
53 Pa.C.S. § 305: municipalities may not regulate the ownership or operation of unmanned aircraft (state preemption), though they may regulate their own drone use.
parks: PA DCNR Bureau of State Parks permits drones only at designated flying sites in six parks: Beltzville, Benjamin Rush, Hillman, Lackawanna, Prompton and Tuscarora (only the designated site, not the whole park). Drones are restricted at all other state park locations; contact the park office first.
https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dcnr/recreation/where-to-go/state-parks/rules-and-regulations/unmanned-aerial-systems-and-drones
DCNR state forest UAS guidelines: no takeoff/landing in designated Natural and Wild Areas; commercial flyers must contact the forest district office.
https://elibrary.dcnr.pa.gov/PDFProvider.ashx?PromptToSave=True&Size=178348&ViewerMode=1&action=PDFStream&chksum=&docID=3411385&docName=Drone+Policy&nativeExt=pdf&overlay=0&revision=0

NY State Parks (OPRHP): launching, landing or operating a drone in state parks and historic sites requires prior written approval via a UAS permit specifying time, place and manner (recreational use under 9 NYCRR 372.7(j)).
https://parks.ny.gov/documents/inside-our-agency/publicdocuments/guidancepolicies/regulatingunmannedaircraftsystemsdronesmodelairplanesquadcopters.pdf
local: New York City: Admin. Code § 10-126(c) bars aircraft takeoffs/landings except at designated places; under NYPD rules (38 RCNY ch. 24) most drone takeoffs/landings need an NYPD permit, generally applied for ~30 days ahead.

laws: 11 Del. C. § 1334: unlawful to knowingly operate a drone over critical infrastructure (e.g., refineries, power plants, electric substations, military facilities, ports, rail yards, water facilities, correctional facilities, government and public-safety buildings), with listed exemptions.
parks: Delaware State Parks: a special-use permit is required to operate a drone on or over land or water administered by DNREC Parks & Recreation (7 DE Admin. Code 9201 § 13); apply through the park superintendent at least 10 days ahead; recreational flights only in designated areas.
https://destateparks.com/Know/Drones

laws: Md. Econ. Dev. Code § 14-301: only the State may regulate testing or operation of unmanned aircraft systems; county and municipal drone laws are preempted.
parks: Maryland DNR: contact the specific state park manager before flying on DNR-managed land; individual parks may add restrictions (e.g., Sandy Point seasonal/hour limits).
https://dnr.maryland.gov/publiclands/Pages/Statewide-Maryland-Park-Policies.aspx
local: Washington DC Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA) covers parts of central Maryland; flying there requires FAA authorization.

laws: Fla. Stat. § 934.50: limits law-enforcement drone surveillance and private drone surveillance of people/private property.
Fla. Stat. § 330.41: protects critical infrastructure facilities from drone operations and preempts local regulation of drone operation (with exceptions).
parks: Florida State Parks: Fla. Admin. Code 62D-2.014(15) bars any aircraft or 'other aerial apparatus' (which the Park Service says includes drones) from taking off or landing in a park except in an emergency or at a designated landing facility; the Park Service says no guest-accessible facilities currently exist. Violations: ejection and fine up to $500 (Fla. Stat. 258.008).
https://www.floridastateparks.org/plan-your-visit/faqs

laws: Cal. Civ. Code § 1708.8: physical invasion of privacy includes knowingly entering the airspace above another's land to capture images/recordings of private activity in an offensive manner.
parks: California State Parks: drones are generally allowed unless prohibited by a District Superintendent's posted order (many districts have one); 14 CCR § 4351 bars motorized equipment incl. drones in State Wilderness, Cultural Preserves and Natural Preserves. Check the park's posted orders.
https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=29229

laws: Tex. Gov't Code § 423.003: Class C misdemeanor to capture an image of an individual or privately owned real property with a drone with intent to conduct surveillance.
Tex. Gov't Code § 423.0045: offense to fly over a critical infrastructure facility below 400 ft, contact it, or interfere with its operations (Class B misdemeanor), with exemptions.
parks: Texas State Parks: drones are allowed only in Martin Dies, Jr. State Park's designated area, or for filming at other parks with a filming permit from the park.
https://tpwd.texas.gov/state-parks/park-information/rules

laws: Va. Code § 15.2-926.3: localities may not regulate privately owned drones, except takeoff/landing on locality-owned property under Dept. of Aviation rules.
Va. Code § 19.2-60.1: law-enforcement/regulatory agencies generally need a warrant to use drones, with listed exceptions.
North Carolina's former state permit and knowledge test for commercial/government drone operators were repealed effective Dec. 1, 2024; commercial ops now follow FAA Part 107.
N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 63, Article 10 (state UAS provisions)

S.C. Code § 24-1-300: no drone within 500 ft horizontally or 250 ft vertically of a Department of Corrections facility without the Director's written consent (misdemeanor). Act 150 of 2026 (H.4679) replaces this with § 55-1-220 and a 1,500-ft buffer effective Jan. 1, 2027.
H.4679 (2025-2026), South Carolina Drone Regulation and Public Safety Act

O.C.G.A. § 6-1-4: preempts local ordinances regulating drone testing or operation (exceptions incl. pre-April 1, 2017 ordinances and launch/landing on public property). HB 58 (2025) added an offense for flying within 400 ft of or over ticketed entertainment events, with exceptions.

parks: Massachusetts DCR properties: 302 CMR 12.04 prohibits taking off or landing an aircraft or 'other apparatus' without a Special Use Permit, except in an emergency. No statewide drone statute is in effect.
https://www.mass.gov/doc/302-cmr-1200-parks-and-recreation-rules/download

laws: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-149b: municipalities generally may not regulate commercial drones flown by FAA-certificated remote pilots; municipal water companies may regulate drones over public water supply land.

Ohio Rev. Code §§ 4561.50-4561.53 (HB 77, 135th GA): drone operators must comply with federal rules; prohibits interfering with on-duty law enforcement, fire and EMS; restricts drone activity at critical facilities; allows local regulation of recreational drones in parks/public property.

Freedom from Drone Surveillance Act, 725 ILCS 167: generally bars law enforcement from gathering information with drones except in listed situations (warrant, emergencies, search and rescue, etc.) and sets data-retention limits.
